Renforcement de la loi 21 : « Ça va seul: Strengthening Bill 21: “It’s only going to add fuel to the fire!”
Le ministre québécois responsable de la: The Quebec minister responsible for secularism has announced the creation of a study committee to strengthen Bill 21.
Le gouvernement caquiste se lance dans u: The CAQ government is launching a battle to protect secularism in Quebec. Jean-François Roberge, the minister responsible for Secularism, first set up a study committee to analyze the situation in Quebec institutions. Bernard Drainville, the minister of Education, then announced that he was tabling a bill to reinforce this Quebec value in schools.
Tous deux prennent comme exemple <l1>l’é: Both point to <l1>the Bedford school</l1> to justify this legislative tightening. My question: why draw a connection between the origin of the suspended teachers at that school, public displays of religion and secularism?
J’ai ainsi recueilli des témoignages de: So I gathered the stories of Muslim women, who consider themselves the people most affected by this process of secularizing institutions.
<strong>Le lundi 10 mars, le ministre qu: On Monday, March 10, the Quebec minister responsible for secularism, Jean-François Roberge, announced the creation of a study committee to strengthen the Act respecting the laicity of the State, or Bill 21. As this project targets the province’s Muslim communities more than ever, we met Maria*, Emy* and Rana Awada, three women who wear the hijab, to give them a voice on the expansion of these measures.
Nous retrouvons Maria, une artiste montr: We meet Maria, a Montréal artist, in her apartment near Little Italy. Once we are comfortably settled, she opens up about her school, professional and personal experience as a veiled woman in Montréal. The subject is delicate, and the emotion is audible in her voice, which trembles slightly.
La pression sociale dont elle a fait l’o: The social pressure she has faced for expressing her faith began early and shaped her educational and professional path. “My experience as a veiled woman during my studies was demoralizing, even before the law was officially introduced,” she says.
Elle se destinait à une carrière d’ensei: She was headed for a career as a philosophy teacher, but the adoption of Bill 21 narrowed her horizons. She then considered going into the field of education, but teachers and classmates discouraged her. “People often made comments to me throughout my journey. It wasn’t always ill-intentioned, but people don’t understand how much it hurts.”
L’histoire de Maria n’est pas un cas iso: Maria’s story is not an isolated case. Throughout her journey, she saw Muslim women give up on teaching careers because they didn’t feel that a place was being left for them in that field.
« Après mes études, je suis allée travai: “After my studies, I went to work in the community sector, with other women who looked like me. I was afraid to go out into the wider world, to confront society and to have to go through situations with non-Muslims that would again be destabilizing, that would remind me that I’m a problem and that I don’t belong in this society,” she says, tears in her eyes.
Aujourd’hui, avec la menace d’élargissem: Today, with the threat of Bill 21 being expanded, Maria feels that pressure even more. “For a lot of Muslim women, there’s this anxiety that’s always present deep down. And this situation really makes it worse,” she says, moved.
Au quotidien, la jeune femme déploie déj: Day to day, the young woman already goes to great lengths to avoid potential attacks linked to wearing the hijab. She no longer takes public transit since she suffered a traumatic physical assault nearly 10 years ago. She carefully chooses the public places where she wears her scarf. Sometimes she even doesn’t wear it, as a safety measure.
« La situation actuelle est tellement dé: “The current situation is so demoralizing and anxiety-inducing. (...) My scarf is so important to me, but the situation is so unbearable that sometimes, when I go out in public, I don’t wear it, and for me, that’s such an act of violence...” says Maria.
Selon la jeune femme, les répercussions: According to the young woman, the repercussions of extending the law will fall above all on the shoulders of Muslim women. They are the ones who have to live with constant pressure and the gaze of others. They are the ones who have to change their way of life and adapt to a society where they feel less and less accepted.
Rappelons que la loi 21, adoptée en juin: As a reminder, Bill 21, adopted in June 2019, prohibits people in positions of authority – such as judges, police officers, prison guards and elementary and secondary school teachers – from wearing religious symbols while performing their duties. The law has prompted numerous court challenges <l1>because of its impact on fundamental freedoms</l1>.
Avec l’élargissement de cette loi, l’int: With the expansion of this law, the ban on wearing religious symbols would apply to all types of private or public educational institutions, hospitals, early childhood centres and much more. For Minister Roberge, the aim is to prevent “religious excesses” within Quebec institutions, but also in public space.
De son côté, le ministre Drainville a pa: For his part, Minister Drainville also announced yesterday that he will table a bill <l1>to strengthen secularism in schools</l1>. In a video posted on social media, he said he was “shaken by what happened at Bedford and in other schools. That is NOT what a Quebec school is,” he declared.
La mise en place du comité d’étude annon: The creation of the study committee announced by the minister responsible for Secularism is notably motivated by the Bedford elementary school affair, which Jean-François Roberge described as a “canary in the coal mine.”
Rappelons qu’en octobre dernier, le mini: As a reminder, last October, Education Minister Bernard Drainville released an investigation report on “a majority clan” of 11 teachers of North African origin who had established “a climate of fear and intimidation” among students and other staff members at Bedford. The teachers were suspended by the Centre de services scolaire de Montréal, and nearly twenty other schools have come under the ministry’s scrutiny.
Mais pourquoi faire le rapprochement ent: But why draw a connection between the origin of these suspended teachers, public displays of religion and secularism?
Zeinab Diab, doctorante en sciences des: Zeinab Diab, a doctoral student in religious studies at Université de Montréal, is not surprised by this push to strengthen Bill 21 and to target the Muslim community. “If it hadn’t been Bedford, there would have been another incident to exploit and feed the secularism discourse. Bill 21 establishes a nationalist political project,” she explains.
« C’est plus facile de dire que c’est l’: “It’s easier to say that Islam is the problem,” she sighs. “We don’t look any further, we don’t get to the root of the problem, which is that the education system is doing worse and worse. For 30 years in Quebec, it’s worked well to say that Muslims are the problem.”
Le comité d’étude annoncé par le ministr: The study committee announced by the minister responsible for Secularism is co-chaired by two lawyers, Christiane Pelchat, former president of the Conseil du statut de la femme, and Guillaume Rousseau, a law professor at Université de Sherbrooke. Its mandate is to verify that the law is being properly applied in various institutions across the province.
Il n’est pas question de consulter les p: There is no question of consulting those most affected for this new stage. No expert in religious studies or sociology and no community member will be at the ministry’s table to discuss it.
<strong>« Si ça continue comme ça, c’est: “If it keeps going like this, I’m definitely leaving Quebec!”
C’est aussi l’avis d’Emy*. Nous la renco: Emy* shares that view. We meet her in a café on Ontario Street. The place is empty, and she speaks openly. We quickly understand that an expansion of Bill 21 could mark a major turning point in her life.
Arrivée d’Algérie à l’âge de cinq ans, e: She arrived from Algeria at the age of five, and remembers her time in elementary school and the catechism classes taught to her classmates. She also remembers the large crosses that decorated the walls of schools and the small silver crosses hanging around her teachers’ necks. It was enough to make her feel a difference in how different religious affiliations were treated: “It’s really a double standard,” she says, discouraged.
Avant de décrocher un poste de directric: Before landing a job as an assistant director at a private daycare, Emy adapted the way she wears the hijab. “Before, I wore the hijab properly, I covered my neck. Now I don’t cover my neck anymore, I wear earrings. I make it a little more stylish. It’s the most I can do to adapt to Quebec society,” she explains.
Mais après plus de 10 ans de carrière da: But after more than 10 years of a career in education and child care, Emy feels a certain unease. She feels that the way she is treated has changed. Since the announcement of the expansion of Bill 21, her family has been considering major changes: “If it keeps going like this, I’m definitely leaving Quebec!” she says sharply. “I’ve only known Quebec in my life. (...) But if they don’t want us, we’ll go elsewhere.”
Comme Emy, Zeinab Diab estime que la soc: Like Emy, Zeinab Diab believes Quebec society holds great uncertainty and a lot of insecurity in store for Muslim women. “They resist, they find strategies to keep existing despite the extremely hostile context. Some go to private schools; they change direction and take other paths. This project thwarts their plan B, their plan C,” she says.
Selon l’intellectuelle, cette initiative: According to the scholar, this legislative initiative will considerably narrow these women’s career choices, isolating them further from life in society. She calls this isolation “social death.”
Pour l’auteure d’une thèse intitulée « R: For the author of a thesis titled “Résister à la loi 21 : Entre mort sociale et stratégies de survie, praxis musulmane et sororité dans une quête de justice sociale” (Resisting Bill 21: Between social death and survival strategies, Muslim praxis and sisterhood in a quest for social justice), the CAQ’s recent drop in the polls is driving and amplifying these nationalist and populist projects. “[The government] wants to give the impression of doing something concrete, something proactive. Yet if you look at education, health care, housing – everything is going badly! But we don’t look at that. We turn to a manufactured problem aimed at Muslim communities.”
Les communautés touchées ne sont cependa: The affected communities are not surprised by such an announcement, however. “The participants in my research tell me: they knew it would go further. We’re very disappointed, but we’re not surprised. It’s been working like this in Quebec for 30 years. With every new election campaign, they pile on another layer!” she observes.
Rana Awada est enseignante dans une écol: Rana Awada is a teacher at a public-sector elementary school. She, for her part, has had few intense experiences related to wearing the hijab in the course of her work.
« Je considère que j’ai eu de la chance: “I consider myself lucky to have had good experiences in the schools where I’ve worked, but it’s still a fight on behalf of all the Muslim women who may or may not be able to work in these conditions,” says Rana.
Sur son compte TikTok, où elle compte pl: On her TikTok account, where she has more than 30,000 followers, she makes a point of expressing her religious identity. She produces content in which she talks about her daily life as a teacher and encourages young people to go into the field. “On social media, I’m often asked: ‘Do you encourage me to keep going despite all the doors that are closing?’ I answer that there are always possibilities when you’re passionate. In my view, there will always be options,” says the teacher.
« C’est dommage que nous ayons un poids: “It’s a shame that we have extra weight to carry. Everyone is supposed to have the same opportunities, given equal skills. It’s all in the head, not around the head!” she adds.
Elle souhaite représenter la communauté: She wants to represent the Muslim community as best she can. “Despite the law being adopted in 2019, I didn’t give up, far from it. I would never have let a law forbid me from doing what I love and being who I am. Today, I’m lucky to be able to make my voice heard in schools and on my platforms. I’ll keep going to the very end,” she says proudly.
Rana évoque certaines inquiétudes à la s: Rana expresses some concerns following the announcement of the expansion of the Act respecting the laicity of the State, but she still wants to represent a source of hope for her community. “If there’s one thing I take away from all this, it’s that giving up our dreams and our opportunities because of a law like this is like proving them right and giving up too easily everything we’re fighting for. To me, it’s important to create opportunities for ourselves, even if they’re taken from us,” she says.
L’incertitude et la combativité sont don: Uncertainty and fighting spirit are therefore the watchwords for the future of women who wear religious symbols in public. “I’m here and I bring the skills I have to the society I live in. I respect others in their differences, in their beliefs and in their practices because that’s part of living together. That’s the step we need to take forward. We still have a long way to go,” concludes Rana.
Questionné sur l’étendue des nouvelles m: Asked about the scope of the new measures being considered, the office of the minister responsible for Secularism referred us to the official press release. No comment will be made on the matter.
